WHO WON THE DAY? Prop 40 opponents , who received good news in the PPIC poll.
WHERE’S GAVIN? In Los Angeles, having a fireside chat with California Science Center CEO Jeffrey Rudolph during a media preview of the Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center.
TOP READS
SHATTERED RECORDS — Billionaire opponents of California’s proposed wealth tax have spent more fighting it than they ever have on a political cause in the state, according to a POLITICO analysis.
A record $612 million from more than 70 current and former California billionaires is flooding this year’s state elections , nearly half of it to groups working to defeat the wealth tax initiative on Tuesday’s ballot, POLITICO found.
The fight over Prop 40 has brought California’s wealthiest residents — many from its native tech industry — together in an unprecedented show of political coordination, the new data reveals. Tech leaders say the wealth tax has accelerated plans for broader political engagement this cycle, building networks that could be the foundation for future campaigns.
Read the full story from Christine Mui and Sean McMinn here (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/28/billionaires-spending-california-wealth-tax-01137778) .
IN THE COURTS
In this Aug. 30, 2021, file photo, mail-in ballots run through a sorting machine at the Sacramento County Registrar of Voters office in Sacramento, California. | Rich Pedroncelli/AP
ELECTION CLAIM SKEPTIC — A federal judge in California signaled Tuesday that he is preparing to reject the Trump administration’s emergency effort to force the state to set aside and review any votes cast by people on a list of 20,000 registered voters the Department of Homeland Security has identified as likely noncitizens.
After a three-hour hearing, U.S. District Judge David Carter instead said he needed a far more extensive briefing on the matter that would extend well past Election Day. In effect, it’s a defeat for the Justice Department, which had demanded the judge immediately force the state to comply. Carter, a Clinton appointee, said DOJ could prosecute anyone it identifies as casting an illegal ballot.
“Of course no one wants a noncitizen voting. Anybody taking that position, it’s a ridiculous position,” he said.
The judge concluded with a stark warning for DOJ, however, after state officials complained that the Trump administration had made menacing comments about potentially prosecuting election workers who tabulated the votes of noncitizens: “This court believes it would be wise that any threats to state and county elected employees cease immediately.”
Carter said he would issue a formal order Wednesday. — Kyle Cheney
First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California Bill Essayli speaks during an announcement at Department of Justice headquarters in Washington on Nov. 19, 2025. | Francis Chung/POLITICO
WHAT’S IN A NAME — A federal judge ruled Tuesday that Bill Essayli is unlawfully acting as a “de facto” U.S. attorney.
Judge J. Michael Seabright , who last year ruled that Essayli was illegally serving in the role (https://www.politico.com/news/2025/10/28/judge-los-angeles-top-federal-prosecutor-illegally-appointed-00626804) of acting U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, wrote that “Essayli—even in his designated role as a Special Attorney and FAUSA—is disqualified from (1) participating in or supervising these cases, or (2) otherwise supervising any attorneys in the handling of these cases.”
Essayli said in a statement that he respectfully disagreed with the ruling.
“The President and the Attorney General have every right to select supervisors within the Justice Department,” he said.
Essayli added that the motion was automatically stayed, and that the status quo will likely remain while the DOJ appeals the decision. “Ultimately, this question will be decided by the Supreme Court,” he said, “and I look forward to serving in my current role until then.” — Nicole Norman
ELECTION YEAR
Chad Bianco speaks during a California gubernatorial debate hosted by CBS Bay Area and the San Francisco Examiner in San Francisco, Thursday, May 14, 2026. | Godofredo A. Vásquez/AP
RELUCTANT SUPPORT? — It was hardly a ringing endorsement, but Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco , who previously declined to endorse (https://www.fresnobee.com/news/politics-government/article315864431.html) Steve Hilton in the governor’s race after losing the primary, voiced support for his fellow Republican’s candidacy on Tuesday.
“I don’t care if you like him or not. We absolutely need Steve Hilton to win this race for governor,” Bianco said in a video on social media (https://x.com/ChadBianco/status/2115188593425850374?a=NXWO74gQaasvSVU-EC4&s=20).
Bianco in May argued (https://www.fresnobee.com/news/politics-government/article315864431.html) that President Donald Trump ’s endorsement of Hilton (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/04/06/before-trump-backed-hilton-loomer-was-already-at-work-00861205) would hurt the former Fox News host in California. But he urged followers to vote for Hilton in the video, anyway, saying “we need balance” amid Democratic rule.
IN THE PHONE BANK — Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas rallied volunteers at a phone bank supporting Democrat Amy Slavensky , telling them her incumbent opponent Assemblymember Josh Hoover is a “nice guy, but he doesn’t represent this community’s interests.” Outgoing Women’s Caucus Chair Cecilia Aguiar-Curry said electing Slavensky, a former school administrator, was a priority of the caucus. And Assemblymember Gail Pellerin , a former local elections official, instructed callers to encourage voters to drop off their ballots in person rather than by mail, citing concerns about possible Trump administration interference.
“We cannot rely on the United States Postal Service right now because they are under the control of this Trump administration, and we don’t want those ballots to get held somewhere and not in the hands of the elections official,” Pellerin told the volunteers gathered in the Sacramento suburb of Fair Oaks.
The event’s attendance by several Democratic officials, including Assemblymember Patrick Ahrens , underscored the force with which their party is trying to oust Hoover despite his moderate profile and, as Rivas seemed to acknowledge, affable demeanor. The state Democratic Party has poured more than $2 million into defeating the frontline Republican, one of several incumbents it’s trying to oust after losing seats in both chambers of the Legislature last cycle.
Super PACs, including the GOP caucus-aligned Legislative Action Victory PAC and another sponsored by CalChamber, have collectively spent more than $3 million defending Hoover and blasting Slavensky.
LOS ANGELES
Los Angeles mayoral candidate Nithya Raman speaks during a campaign event on Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026, in Sylmar, California. | William Liang/AP
POWER PLAY — Frustration over sky-high electricity bills is becoming a flashpoint in the closing days of the Los Angeles mayor’s race, with Karen Bass and her progressive challenger, Nithya Raman , trading blows over utility costs that have soared amid record-breaking heatwaves, Alex Nieves reports for subscribers (https://subscriber.politicopro.com/article/2026/10/the-la-mayors-race-goes-electric-01137758).
The fracas began early last week after Raman held a press conference alongside frustrated Los Angeles Department of Water and Power customers, where the council member blamed Bass for letting the utility raise electricity and water rates without City Council approval — and promised to audit the department. Bass has responded with promises to lower bills and investigate the city’s climbing utility costs.
The last-minute brawl comes as candidates statewide contend with high electricity prices and broader concerns about the cost of living — an issue (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) which is among voters’ top concerns. California’s electricity rates are the second-highest in the U.S., behind only Hawaii. Read last night’s California Currents (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-currents/2026/10/27/ramans-electric-closing-message-01137445) to see how both campaigns are trying to navigate energy affordability angst ahead of Election Day.
Top Talkers
UCLA SUIT — For the second time this month, the University of California has asked a federal judge to dismiss a lawsuit by the Department of Justice alleging that UCLA failed to properly address antisemitic incidents during protests over Israel’s war against Hamas.
In a motion filed later Monday, UC officials acknowledged that “there is no question that some University employees were exposed to antisemitism on campus” but called the Trump administration’s claims of a campus overrun by it “flawed,” Eric He reports for subscribers (https://subscriber.politicopro.com/article/2026/10/uc-seeks-to-dismiss-another-doj-antisemitism-lawsuit-01136943).

DOWNWARD ARC — Where a campaign stands matters less than where it’s headed — and less than a week from the election, major ballot initiatives are losing ground.
The trendlines are troubling for Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time wealth tax on California’s billionaires, and for Proposition 45, which would streamline environmental reviews for construction projects. Support for both measures has slipped markedly in the last month, according to the Public Policy Institute of California (http://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/), as ballots hit mailboxes and millions of dollars in negative ads inundated the airwaves.
The wealth tax has seen an especially big swing: Support fell from 52% in September to 46% this month, while opposition rose from 46% to 52% — the first time a prominent public poll has found a majority of voters opposing the measure. But Prop 45 also plunged underwater. Opposition leads 50-46, reversing the measure’s 49-46 advantage in PPIC’s September poll.
Both measures eroded as opponents assailed their weak spots. Critics of Prop 45, which would change California’s environmental review law, have warned the measure could expedite the building of fossil fuel infrastructure and increasingly unpopular data centers. Opponents of the wealth tax have argued it could eventually be expanded to hit working Californians. Supporters disputed both claims.
PROP 3 HOLDS — The wealth tax’s slide in the polls hasn’t extended to Proposition 3, which would make permanent an existing tax on top earners to fund education. Support for that measure held steady at 58%, a result that may ease union proponents’ fears that opposition to Proposition 40 could spill over to Prop 3.
Those divergent trendlines reflected starkly different political and financial realities. The Prop 3 campaign has raised more than $80 million and faced no funded opposition; the wealth tax effort has operated on a shoestring budget as billionaires spend hundreds of millions of dollars against it. Democrats are largely unified behind Prop 3, while Prop 40 has been extraordinarily divisive within the party.
Prop 40 was not the only SEIU-UHW-championed measure to backslide as opponents piled on. Support for Proposition 44, which would regulate clinics, shrank to just 25% in the face of a $44 million health care industry counteroffensive. In both cases, SEIU-UHW spent millions on qualification but has not followed up with a comparable advertising campaign.
Two billionaire-funded measures designed to torpedo Prop 40 were also on the bubble amid tightening polling: Proposition 41 declined from a 51-44 majority in September to 48-49 this month, and Proposition 42 went from 54-43 to 51-47. Wealthy backers have largely focused on 42, pouring some $65 million into the campaign this month. But the rest of the ballot is looking increasingly predictable as campaigns either held steady or saw polling gaps expand.
THE REST OF THE BALLOT — Voters broadly support two housing bonds (Proposition 1 and Proposition 37), an expansion of the state’s “rainy day” reserve fund (Proposition 2), and an immunology research bond (Proposition 38). A voter ID measure (Proposition 39) and an initiative making it harder to raise local taxes (Proposition 43) are both trailing by double-digit margins. And two measures to institute public election financing (Proposition 4) and overhaul recalls (Proposition 5) remain below majority support despite creeping up to 45%.

SHATTERED RECORDS — Billionaire opponents of California’s proposed wealth tax have spent more fighting it than they ever have on a political cause in the state, according to a POLITICO analysis.
A record $612 million from more than 70 current and former California billionaires is flooding this year’s state elections , nearly half of it to groups working to defeat the wealth tax initiative on Tuesday’s ballot, POLITICO found.
The fight over Prop 40 has brought California’s wealthiest residents — many from its native tech industry — together in an unprecedented show of political coordination, the new data reveals. Tech leaders say the wealth tax has accelerated plans for broader political engagement this cycle, building networks that could be the foundation for future campaigns.

In this Aug. 30, 2021, file photo, mail-in ballots run through a sorting machine at the Sacramento County Registrar of Voters office in Sacramento, California. | Rich Pedroncelli/AP
ELECTION CLAIM SKEPTIC — A federal judge in California signaled Tuesday that he is preparing to reject the Trump administration’s emergency effort to force the state to set aside and review any votes cast by people on a list of 20,000 registered voters the Department of Homeland Security has identified as likely noncitizens.
After a three-hour hearing, U.S. District Judge David Carter instead said he needed a far more extensive briefing on the matter that would extend well past Election Day. In effect, it’s a defeat for the Justice Department, which had demanded the judge immediately force the state to comply. Carter, a Clinton appointee, said DOJ could prosecute anyone it identifies as casting an illegal ballot.
“Of course no one wants a noncitizen voting. Anybody taking that position, it’s a ridiculous position,” he said.
The judge concluded with a stark warning for DOJ, however, after state officials complained that the Trump administration had made menacing comments about potentially prosecuting election workers who tabulated the votes of noncitizens: “This court believes it would be wise that any threats to state and county elected employees cease immediately.”
Carter said he would issue a formal order Wednesday. — Kyle Cheney
First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California Bill Essayli speaks during an announcement at Department of Justice headquarters in Washington on Nov. 19, 2025. | Francis Chung/POLITICO
WHAT’S IN A NAME — A federal judge ruled Tuesday that Bill Essayli is unlawfully acting as a “de facto” U.S. attorney.
Judge J. Michael Seabright , who last year ruled that Essayli was illegally serving in the role (https://www.politico.com/news/2025/10/28/judge-los-angeles-top-federal-prosecutor-illegally-appointed-00626804) of acting U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, wrote that “Essayli—even in his designated role as a Special Attorney and FAUSA—is disqualified from (1) participating in or supervising these cases, or (2) otherwise supervising any attorneys in the handling of these cases.”
Essayli said in a statement that he respectfully disagreed with the ruling.

DOWNWARD ARC — Where a campaign stands matters less than where it’s headed — and less than a week from the election, major ballot initiatives are losing ground.
The trendlines are troubling for Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time wealth tax on California’s billionaires, and for Proposition 45, which would streamline environmental reviews for construction projects. Support for both measures has slipped markedly in the last month, according to the Public Policy Institute of California (http://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/), as ballots hit mailboxes and millions of dollars in negative ads inundated the airwaves.
The wealth tax has seen an especially big swing: Support fell from 52% in September to 46% this month, while opposition rose from 46% to 52% — the first time a prominent public poll has found a majority of voters opposing the measure. But Prop 45 also plunged underwater. Opposition leads 50-46, reversing the measure’s 49-46 advantage in PPIC’s September poll.
Both measures eroded as opponents assailed their weak spots. Critics of Prop 45, which would change California’s environmental review law, have warned the measure could expedite the building of fossil fuel infrastructure and increasingly unpopular data centers. Opponents of the wealth tax have argued it could eventually be expanded to hit working Californians. Supporters disputed both claims.
PROP 3 HOLDS — The wealth tax’s slide in the polls hasn’t extended to Proposition 3, which would make permanent an existing tax on top earners to fund education. Support for that measure held steady at 58%, a result that may ease union proponents’ fears that opposition to Proposition 40 could spill over to Prop 3.
Those divergent trendlines reflected starkly different political and financial realities. The Prop 3 campaign has raised more than $80 million and faced no funded opposition; the wealth tax effort has operated on a shoestring budget as billionaires spend hundreds of millions of dollars against it. Democrats are largely unified behind Prop 3, while Prop 40 has been extraordinarily divisive within the party.
Prop 40 was not the only SEIU-UHW-championed measure to backslide as opponents piled on. Support for Proposition 44, which would regulate clinics, shrank to just 25% in the face of a $44 million health care industry counteroffensive. In both cases, SEIU-UHW spent millions on qualification but has not followed up with a comparable advertising campaign.
Two billionaire-funded measures designed to torpedo Prop 40 were also on the bubble amid tightening polling: Proposition 41 declined from a 51-44 majority in September to 48-49 this month, and Proposition 42 went from 54-43 to 51-47. Wealthy backers have largely focused on 42, pouring some $65 million into the campaign this month. But the rest of the ballot is looking increasingly predictable as campaigns either held steady or saw polling gaps expand.
THE REST OF THE BALLOT — Voters broadly support two housing bonds (Proposition 1 and Proposition 37), an expansion of the state’s “rainy day” reserve fund (Proposition 2), and an immunology research bond (Proposition 38). A voter ID measure (Proposition 39) and an initiative making it harder to raise local taxes (Proposition 43) are both trailing by double-digit margins. And two measures to institute public election financing (Proposition 4) and overhaul recalls (Proposition 5) remain below majority support despite creeping up to 45%.

DOWNWARD ARC — Where a campaign stands matters less than where it’s headed — and less than a week from the election, major ballot initiatives are losing ground.
The trendlines are troubling for Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time wealth tax on California’s billionaires, and for Proposition 45, which would streamline environmental reviews for construction projects. Support for both measures has slipped markedly in the last month, according to the Public Policy Institute of California (http://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/), as ballots hit mailboxes and millions of dollars in negative ads inundated the airwaves.
The wealth tax has seen an especially big swing: Support fell from 52% in September to 46% this month, while opposition rose from 46% to 52% — the first time a prominent public poll has found a majority of voters opposing the measure. But Prop 45 also plunged underwater. Opposition leads 50-46, reversing the measure’s 49-46 advantage in PPIC’s September poll.
Both measures eroded as opponents assailed their weak spots. Critics of Prop 45, which would change California’s environmental review law, have warned the measure could expedite the building of fossil fuel infrastructure and increasingly unpopular data centers. Opponents of the wealth tax have argued it could eventually be expanded to hit working Californians. Supporters disputed both claims.
PROP 3 HOLDS — The wealth tax’s slide in the polls hasn’t extended to Proposition 3, which would make permanent an existing tax on top earners to fund education. Support for that measure held steady at 58%, a result that may ease union proponents’ fears that opposition to Proposition 40 could spill over to Prop 3.
Those divergent trendlines reflected starkly different political and financial realities. The Prop 3 campaign has raised more than $80 million and faced no funded opposition; the wealth tax effort has operated on a shoestring budget as billionaires spend hundreds of millions of dollars against it. Democrats are largely unified behind Prop 3, while Prop 40 has been extraordinarily divisive within the party.
Prop 40 was not the only SEIU-UHW-championed measure to backslide as opponents piled on. Support for Proposition 44, which would regulate clinics, shrank to just 25% in the face of a $44 million health care industry counteroffensive. In both cases, SEIU-UHW spent millions on qualification but has not followed up with a comparable advertising campaign.
Two billionaire-funded measures designed to torpedo Prop 40 were also on the bubble amid tightening polling: Proposition 41 declined from a 51-44 majority in September to 48-49 this month, and Proposition 42 went from 54-43 to 51-47. Wealthy backers have largely focused on 42, pouring some $65 million into the campaign this month. But the rest of the ballot is looking increasingly predictable as campaigns either held steady or saw polling gaps expand.
THE REST OF THE BALLOT — Voters broadly support two housing bonds (Proposition 1 and Proposition 37), an expansion of the state’s “rainy day” reserve fund (Proposition 2), and an immunology research bond (Proposition 38). A voter ID measure (Proposition 39) and an initiative making it harder to raise local taxes (Proposition 43) are both trailing by double-digit margins. And two measures to institute public election financing (Proposition 4) and overhaul recalls (Proposition 5) remain below majority support despite creeping up to 45%.

SHATTERED RECORDS — Billionaire opponents of California’s proposed wealth tax have spent more fighting it than they ever have on a political cause in the state, according to a POLITICO analysis.
A record $612 million from more than 70 current and former California billionaires is flooding this year’s state elections , nearly half of it to groups working to defeat the wealth tax initiative on Tuesday’s ballot, POLITICO found.
The fight over Prop 40 has brought California’s wealthiest residents — many from its native tech industry — together in an unprecedented show of political coordination, the new data reveals. In this Aug. 30, 2021, file photo, mail-in ballots run through a sorting machine at the Sacramento County Registrar of Voters office in Sacramento, California. | Rich Pedroncelli/AP
ELECTION CLAIM SKEPTIC — A federal judge in California signaled Tuesday that he is preparing to reject the Trump administration’s emergency effort to force the state to set aside and review any votes cast by people on a list of 20,000 registered voters the Department of Homeland Security has identified as likely noncitizens.
After a three-hour hearing, U.S. District Judge David Carter instead said he needed a far more extensive briefing on the matter that would extend well past Election Day. In effect, it’s a defeat for the Justice Department, which had demanded the judge immediately force the state to comply. Carter, a Clinton appointee, said DOJ could prosecute anyone it identifies as casting an illegal ballot.
“Of course no one wants a noncitizen voting. Anybody taking that position, it’s a ridiculous position,” he said.
The judge concluded with a stark warning for DOJ, however, after state officials complained that the Trump administration had made menacing comments about potentially prosecuting election workers who tabulated the votes of noncitizens: “This court believes it would be wise that any threats to state and county elected employees cease immediately.”
Carter said he would issue a formal order Wednesday. — Kyle Cheney
First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California Bill Essayli speaks during an announcement at Department of Justice headquarters in Washington on Nov. 19, 2025. | Francis Chung/POLITICO
WHAT’S IN A NAME — A federal judge ruled Tuesday that Bill Essayli is unlawfully acting as a “de facto” U.S. attorney.
Judge J. Michael Seabright , who last year ruled that Essayli was illegally serving in the role (https://www.politico.com/news/2025/10/28/judge-los-angeles-top-federal-prosecutor-illegally-appointed-00626804) of acting U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, wrote that “Essayli—even in his designated role as a Special Attorney and FAUSA—is disqualified from (1) participating in or supervising these cases, or (2) otherwise supervising any attorneys in the handling of these cases.”
Essayli said in a statement that he respectfully disagreed with the ruling.
“The President and the Attorney General have every right to select supervisors within the Justice Department,” he said.
Essayli added that the motion was automatically stayed, and that the status quo will likely remain while the DOJ appeals the decision. “Ultimately, this question will be decided by the Supreme Court,” he said, “and I look forward to serving in my current role until then.” — Nicole Norman

Chad Bianco speaks during a California gubernatorial debate hosted by CBS Bay Area and the San Francisco Examiner in San Francisco, Thursday, May 14, 2026. | Godofredo A. Vásquez/AP
RELUCTANT SUPPORT? — It was hardly a ringing endorsement, but Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco , who previously declined to endorse (https://www.fresnobee.com/news/politics-government/article315864431.html) Steve Hilton in the governor’s race after losing the primary, voiced support for his fellow Republican’s candidacy on Tuesday.
“I don’t care if you like him or not. We absolutely need Steve Hilton to win this race for governor,” Bianco said in a video on social media (https://x.com/ChadBianco/status/2115188593425850374?a=NXWO74gQaasvSVU-EC4&s=20).
Bianco in May argued (https://www.fresnobee.com/news/politics-government/article315864431.html) that President Donald Trump ’s endorsement of Hilton (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/04/06/before-trump-backed-hilton-loomer-was-already-at-work-00861205) would hurt the former Fox News host in California. But he urged followers to vote for Hilton in the video, anyway, saying “we need balance” amid Democratic rule.
IN THE PHONE BANK — Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas rallied volunteers at a phone bank supporting Democrat Amy Slavensky , telling them her incumbent opponent Assemblymember Josh Hoover is a “nice guy, but he doesn’t represent this community’s interests.” Outgoing Women’s Caucus Chair Cecilia Aguiar-Curry said electing Slavensky, a former school administrator, was a priority of the caucus. And Assemblymember Gail Pellerin , a former local elections official, instructed callers to encourage voters to drop off their ballots in person rather than by mail, citing concerns about possible Trump administration interference.
“We cannot rely on the United States Postal Service right now because they are under the control of this Trump administration, and we don’t want those ballots to get held somewhere and not in the hands of the elections official,” Pellerin told the volunteers gathered in the Sacramento suburb of Fair Oaks.
The event’s attendance by several Democratic officials, including Assemblymember Patrick Ahrens , underscored the force with which their party is trying to oust Hoover despite his moderate profile and, as Rivas seemed to acknowledge, affable demeanor. The state Democratic Party has poured more than $2 million into defeating the frontline Republican, one of several incumbents it’s trying to oust after losing seats in both chambers of the Legislature last cycle.
Super PACs, including the GOP caucus-aligned Legislative Action Victory PAC and another sponsored by CalChamber, have collectively spent more than $3 million defending Hoover and blasting Slavensky.

POWER PLAY — Frustration over sky-high electricity bills is becoming a flashpoint in the closing days of the Los Angeles mayor’s race, with Karen Bass and her progressive challenger, Nithya Raman , trading blows over utility costs that have soared amid record-breaking heatwaves, Alex Nieves reports for subscribers (https://subscriber.politicopro.com/article/2026/10/the-la-mayors-race-goes-electric-01137758).
The fracas began early last week after Raman held a press conference alongside frustrated Los Angeles Department of Water and Power customers, where the council member blamed Bass for letting the utility raise electricity and water rates without City Council approval — and promised to audit the department. Bass has responded with promises to lower bills and investigate the city’s climbing utility costs.
The last-minute brawl comes as candidates statewide contend with high electricity prices and broader concerns about the cost of living — an issue (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) which is among voters’ top concerns. assistantMessageEvent.content:
I found no official results, so this is a prediction for the November 3, 2026 vote on Prop 44, which would require community health clinics to spend 90% of their revenue on program services. The "no" side is far more likely to win.

- **Polls:** PPIC found 34% yes and 61% no among likely voters in September. By October 16–22 it was 25% yes and 71% no, with at least six in ten voting no in every party, demographic group and region.
- **Money:** Opponents raised about $38.6 million and the backers about $16.9 million, most of it spent getting the measure on the ballot. The sponsoring union, SEIU-UHW, spent only about $20,000 on the campaign between July 1 and September 19.
- **Opposition:** Against it are both state parties, the governor, the California Medical Association, the teachers' union, Planned Parenthood and more than 300 groups and 1,000 clinics. The union is the measure's only major backer.
- **History:** Voters rejected all three of the same union's dialysis-clinic measures (2018, 2020 and 2022) by wide margins.
- **Forecast:** On Point Politics' model gives it about a 0.1% chance of passing.

REQUIRES COMMUNITY HEALTH CLINICS SPEND 90% OF REVENUE ON PROGRAM SERVICES. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Imposes penalties on nonprofit Federally Qualified Health Centers (community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations) that spend less than 90% of revenue on “program services” advancing their charitable purpose, including but not limited to patient services. Fiscal Impact: Increased state costs in the low tens of millions of dollars per year, covered by fees. Supporters: None submitted Opponents: American Academy of Pediatrics CA; CA School Nurses Org; CA Academy of Family Physicians; CA Medical Assoc.
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would have to spend at least 90 percent of their revenue each year on providing health care services.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The new requirement on health care clinic spending would not go into effect.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Prop. 44 holds community clinics and their executives accountable by requiring that 90% of clinic revenue be spent on clinics’ charitable mission: patient care and services that make care possible. It increases transparency, reduces wasteful executive spending, and ensures healthcare dollars go where they belong: caring for Californians in need.
CON
Prop. 44 is a dangerous measure that will shut down hundreds of community health clinics and eliminate vital patient services for millions of Californians. I'm checking whether SEIU-UHW had other health-care measures pulled after deals, and I'm wondering why they'd target community clinics with Prop 44. Since the measure has a proposition number, it has cleared the withdrawal deadline and will stay on the ballot.

I'm weighing whether Prop 44 is likely to pass, and my starting point is that SEIU-UHW's health-care measures opposed by doctors and clinic groups have usually failed. A forgotten ballot measure? Union behind billionaire tax spends little on Prop. 44
By Ben Paviour
October 19, 2026 5:00 AM
Critics of Proposition 44 hold signs at a meeting of the resolutions committee of the California Democratic Party’s Executive Committee on Aug. 1, 2026. The measure would place new restrictions on how California’s federally-funded healthcare clinics spend money.
Ben Paviour
ben.paviour@sacbee.com
The union that put the billionaire tax on the ballot has put little money behind its other measure, Proposition 44 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317016992.html), a low-polling measure focused on health clinic spending.
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West spent a little more than $20,000 on Prop. 44 from July 1 to Sept. 19, according to its most recent campaign filings, while opponents spent more than $32 million in the same period.
The SEIU-UHW appears to have concentrated its limited resources onProp. 40, a nationally-watched effort (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317075667.html) to impose a one-time, 5% tax on billionaires’ wealth to offset federal healthcare cuts. The “Yes on 40” campaign spent $4.4 million during the period — still less than 10% of the total spent by billionaire tax opponents.
A Public Policy Institute of California poll released in mid-September (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0926.pdf) found Prop. 44 was the least popular propositions surveyed, with 34% of likely voters saying they supported the measure. Prop. 40, on the other hand, showed 52% support, though subsequent surveys have showed lower levels of support.
Prop. 44 would require federally-funded health clinics to spend 90% of their revenues on patient services, a move SEIU-UHW says would strengthen accountability. Critics like the California Primary Care Association argue the measure is poorly designed and was sponsored by SEIU-UHW President Dave Regan to win concessions from clinics SEIU-UHW is seeking to unionize.
Last month, the CPCA and five clinics filed a lawsuit accusing Regan and his union of racketeering. They argued he launches “punitive, harmful, and often long-shot and repetitive statewide or local ballot initiatives that are used as bargaining chips to extort broad concessions.” The case has yet to be heard.
The CPCA filed a lawsuit in April seeking to keep Prop. 44 off the ballot. A federal judge dismissed the case in August, saying the plaintiffs lacked standing.
Loading…
SEIU-UHW spokesperson Renée Saldaña said the union had not abandoned Prop. 44 and denied that bringing it was a negotiating tactic, calling the allegations in the latest lawsuit “categorically false.”
“Our path to victory is making sure voters understand what Prop 44 does: with federal cuts putting enormous pressure on California’s healthcare system, it ensures clinics that receive public funding spend that money on patient care,” Saldaña said. “SEIU-UHW members will be making that case through Election Day.”
No on 44 spokesperson Molly Weedn said they remained committed to defeating the measure.
“It’s shameful that UHW would put such a dangerous measure on the ballot and force community clinics to mount a campaign to defeat it, especially when there is so much work to do in communities ensuring people are getting the healthcare they need and deserve,” Weedn said in an email.

### Summary
On May 18, 2026, the Secretary of State determined through a random sample that the measure had enough valid signatures to become eligible for the ballot.
It was formally certified for the November 3, 2026, statewide ballot on June 25, 2026, and subsequently designated Proposition 44.
Proposition 44 would require certain private nonprofit safety net clinics in California to spend at least 90% of their total revenue each year on providing health care services.
No more than 10% could be spent on administrative and other expenses that do not qualify as health care services.
The California Attorney General would establish more comprehensive rules for determining which expenses count toward the 90% requirement, and affected clinics could seek temporary waivers in certain circumstances.
Clinics that fail to meet the 90% spending requirement would have to pay a penalty to the state for an amount equal to the shortfall.
The clinic could be reimbursed if it comes into compliance within five years.
If it does not meet the requirements, the state would keep the money and use it to support workforce programs for safety net clinics.

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days.
Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and
state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition,
the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of
these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind,
with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on
topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’
initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race.
Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63%
to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the
Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six
percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic
about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1
(60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three
legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title
and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37
(65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and
Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and
support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at
least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least
“somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and
the economy as well as housing costs and availability as
the most important issues facing California today.
Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is
headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming
majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in
the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49
percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults
and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big
problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of
confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
3/40
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At
the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52
House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters
will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’
initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter
engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton
(R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led
Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (61% to 36%).
Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats
support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the
Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra
over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions
and threats to democratic values and norms as the most
important problems facing the nation today.
Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think
the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and
expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next
12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President
Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action
against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is
working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for
Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
4/40
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the
November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the
gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey), the 2022 general
election (62% October 2022 survey), and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey). Today,
majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of
independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with
the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions
are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election
(22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following
news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten
were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (25% very,
35% fairly) and in October 2018 (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69%
Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters
(65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic
candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were
similar in September (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (64%
Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more
Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most
independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to
37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic
candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
5/40
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are
more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half
or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an
“enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and
between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-
one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, shortly before the
June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024, ahead of the last congressional
election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more
enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature
placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say
they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds
for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey, 55 percent said
they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan
groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54%
to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition
1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on
this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014;
38 percent would vote no. In the September survey, 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent
would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23%
Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age,
gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns). Forty-five percent of
likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local
governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the
6/40
When we asked likely voters which of the 14 state propositions they are most interested in, 14 percent chose
one of the five legislative ballot measures (7% Proposition 1; 1% Proposition 2; 2% Proposition 4; 2%
Proposition 5; 2% Proposition 43). Eighty-six percent are most interested in one of the nine citizens’
initiatives, with about half expressing the most interest in Proposition 39 (23%; Prohibits Citizens from Voting
Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) and Proposition 40 (22%; Imposes One-Time Tax).
There are partisan divides in interest in Proposition 39 (13% Democrat, 47% Republican, 16% independents)
and Proposition 40 (27% Democrats, 13% Republicans, 21% independents). Since the September survey, the
share of those most interested in Proposition 40 has increased (16% to 22%).
September survey, 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for
Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and
declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in
the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters
say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies
be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the September
survey, 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition
5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50
percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services). Forty-two
percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which
increases the percentage of voters needed to approve local special taxes from a majority to two-thirds; 55
percent would vote no. In the September survey, 43 percent said they would vote yes and 51 percent would
vote no. Today, support for Proposition 43 varies across partisan groups (28% Democrats, 68% Republicans,
41% independents) and age groups (30% 18 to 34; 37% 35 to 54; 50% 55 and older) and is below 50
percent across regions.
7/40
Citizens’ Initiatives on the November Ballot
In addition to the five legislative measures, voters are weighing in on nine citizens’ initiatives. Overwhelming
majorities of California likely voters say that the voter information guide, which is mailed to voters by the
California Secretary of State, is very (40%) or somewhat useful (48%; 12% not too useful). Most are very (26%)
8/40
or somewhat satisfied (59%) with the information that is available to voters about citizens’ initiatives on the
state ballot (14% not satisfied).
After reading the ballot title and label for Proposition 3 (Extending Tax on High Incomes), which would make
temporary voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 permanent, a majority of likely
voters in the state say they would vote yes; four in ten would vote no. Findings were similar in September
2026 (58% yes, 40% no). Today, most Democrats and independents support Proposition 3, while most
Republicans oppose. Likely voters who earn less than $40,000 (77%), are age 18 to 34 (73%), or are renters
(69%) are among the most likely to say they would vote yes. Majorities across regions are in support, though
Central Valley residents are more divided (51% yes, 48% no).
Proposition 37 (Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Home-Buyers), which would authorize $25 billion
in bonds to offer eligible California residents fixed-rate mortgages for newly constructed homes below $1.5
million, is supported by about two in three likely voters (65% yes, 32% no). Support was similar in September
(61% yes, 35% no). Majorities of Democrats (80%) and independents (54%) are in support; Republicans are
more divided (47% yes, 51% no). Majorities across demographic and regional groups say they would vote
yes on Proposition 37, and support declines with rising age and income.
A majority of likely voters (57%) would vote yes on Proposition 38 (Authorizes Bonds For Immunology
Medical Research), which would authorize $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds. About four in ten would
vote no (41%). The share in support is similar to a month ago (55% yes, September 2026). Today, partisans
are divided (70% Democrats, 53% independents, 37% Republicans) and majorities across regions and
demographic groups are in support of Proposition 38.
Fewer than half of likely voters in the state would vote yes (41%, 58% no) on Proposition 39 (Prohibits
Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) which would invalidate mail
ballots that do not have the last four digits of a government-issued identification number written on the
envelope and prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Shares were
similar a month ago (43% yes, 55% no). Today, most Republicans would vote yes (82%), most Democrats
9/40
would vote no (84%), and independents are divided (48% yes, 50% no). Majorities across most demographic
groups would vote no, except for likely voters whose highest level of education is a high school diploma,
who are more divided (48% yes, 49% no).
Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax), which would impose a 5 percent tax on certain taxpayers with
assets over $1 billion, is supported by 46 percent of likely voters, while 52 percent would vote no. A slim
majority was in support in September (52% yes, 46% no). Today, over six in ten Democrats would vote yes,
compared to four in ten independents and about two in ten Republicans. Likely voters who are younger
(70% 18 to 34), earn less than $40,000 (64%), are Latino (58%), or reside in Los Angeles (53%) are among the
most likely to support this proposition.
Likely voters are divided on Proposition 41 (Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State
Spending Limit), which would nullify state taxes enacted after January 1 this year that exempt their revenues
from the voter-approved state spending limit and requires audits of programs funded by new special taxes
(48% yes, 49% no). Support was similar in September (51% yes, 44% no). Today, most Republicans and
independents support Proposition 41, compared to about three in ten Democrats. Support varies across
demographic and regional groups.
A slim majority of likely voters would vote yes (51%, 47% no) on Proposition 42 (Prohibits New State Personal
Property Taxes), which would prohibit new state taxes imposed on the ownership of personal property other
than real estate. Support was similar a month ago (54% yes, 43% no). Today, most Republicans and
independents would vote yes, while most Democrats would vote no. The share in support varies across
demographic and regional groups.
Just a quarter of likely voters would vote yes (25%, 71% no) on Proposition 44 (Requires Community Health
Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services), which would impose penalties on nonprofit
community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations that spend less
than 90 percent of revenue on program services. A majority was opposed in September (34% yes, 61% no).
Today, six in ten or more across partisan, demographic, and regional groups would vote no.
10/40
Likely voters are divided (46% yes, 50% no) on Proposition 45 (Modifies Environmental Review), which
would amend the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain
projects by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project
approvals. Views were similar a month ago (49% yes, 46% no). A majority of Republicans would vote yes,
while a majority of Democrats (54%) and half of independents (50%) would vote no. The shares in support
vary across partisan, demographic, and regional groups.
11/40
12/40
State of the State
Ahead of the November election, about four in ten adults (45%) and likely voters (38%) choose cost of living,
inflation, and the economy as the most important issue facing people in California today. Fewer choose
housing costs and availability (12% adults, 13% likely voters). Cost of living is most likely to be chosen as the
state’s top issue across parties, regions, and demographic groups.
When asked about the economic outlook for the next 12 months, most Californians are pessimistic, with
three in four adults (77%) and likely voters (79%) expecting bad economic times. Seven in ten Californians
have held this view since 2025. Today, two in three or more across parties, regions, and demographic

California's community health clinics are facing a 90% spending rule under Proposition 44, which would penalize nonprofit clinics that spend less on patient services.
Proposition 44 would require California's nonprofit community health clinics to spend at least 90% of their revenue each year on patient services and the work that supports them, or pay the difference to the state as a penalty.
The clinics it covers are Federally Qualified Health Centers: the network of safety-net clinics that provide primary, dental and mental health care to low-income and uninsured patients, many of them on Medi-Cal.
Prop 44 is an initiative statute placed on the ballot by petition, and its sponsor and sole funder is SEIU United Healthcare Workers West, a health care workers union.

DOWNWARD ARC — Where a campaign stands matters less than where it’s headed — and less than a week from the election, major ballot initiatives are losing ground.
The trendlines are troubling for Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time wealth tax on California’s billionaires, and for Proposition 45, which would streamline environmental reviews for construction projects. Support for both measures has slipped markedly in the last month, according to the Public Policy Institute of California (http://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/), as ballots hit mailboxes and millions of dollars in negative ads inundated the airwaves.
The wealth tax has seen an especially big swing: Support fell from 52% in September to 46% this month, while opposition rose from 46% to 52% — the first time a prominent public poll has found a majority of voters opposing the measure. But Prop 45 also plunged underwater. Opposition leads 50-46, reversing the measure’s 49-46 advantage in PPIC’s September poll.
Both measures eroded as opponents assailed their weak spots. Critics of Prop 45, which would change California’s environmental review law, have warned the measure could expedite the building of fossil fuel infrastructure and increasingly unpopular data centers. Opponents of the wealth tax have argued it could eventually be expanded to hit working Californians. Supporters disputed both claims.
PROP 3 HOLDS — The wealth tax’s slide in the polls hasn’t extended to Proposition 3, which would make permanent an existing tax on top earners to fund education. Support for that measure held steady at 58%, a result that may ease union proponents’ fears that opposition to Proposition 40 could spill over to Prop 3.
Those divergent trendlines reflected starkly different political and financial realities. The Prop 3 campaign has raised more than $80 million and faced no funded opposition; the wealth tax effort has operated on a shoestring budget as billionaires spend hundreds of millions of dollars against it. Democrats are largely unified behind Prop 3, while Prop 40 has been extraordinarily divisive within the party.
Prop 40 was not the only SEIU-UHW-championed measure to backslide as opponents piled on. Support for Proposition 44, which would regulate clinics, shrank to just 25% in the face of a $44 million health care industry counteroffensive. In both cases, SEIU-UHW spent millions on qualification but has not followed up with a comparable advertising campaign.
Two billionaire-funded measures designed to torpedo Prop 40 were also on the bubble amid tightening polling: Proposition 41 declined from a 51-44 majority in September to 48-49 this month, and Proposition 42 went from 54-43 to 51-47. Wealthy backers have largely focused on 42, pouring some $65 million into the campaign this month. But the rest of the ballot is looking increasingly predictable as campaigns either held steady or saw polling gaps expand.
THE REST OF THE BALLOT — Voters broadly support two housing bonds (Proposition 1 and Proposition 37), an expansion of the state’s “rainy day” reserve fund (Proposition 2), and an immunology research bond (Proposition 38). A voter ID measure (Proposition 39) and an initiative making it harder to raise local taxes (Proposition 43) are both trailing by double-digit margins. And two measures to institute public election financing (Proposition 4) and overhaul recalls (Proposition 5) remain below majority support despite creeping up to 45%.

SHATTERED RECORDS — Billionaire opponents of California’s proposed wealth tax have spent more fighting it than they ever have on a political cause in the state, according to a POLITICO analysis.
A record $612 million from more than 70 current and former California billionaires is flooding this year’s state elections , nearly half of it to groups working to defeat the wealth tax initiative on Tuesday’s ballot, POLITICO found.
The fight over Prop 40 has brought California’s wealthiest residents — many from its native tech industry — together in an unprecedented show of political coordination, the new data reveals. After a three-hour hearing, U.S. District Judge David Carter instead said he needed a far more extensive briefing on the matter that would extend well past Election Day. In effect, it’s a defeat for the Justice Department, which had demanded the judge immediately force the state to comply. Carter, a Clinton appointee, said DOJ could prosecute anyone it identifies as casting an illegal ballot.
“Of course no one wants a noncitizen voting. Anybody taking that position, it’s a ridiculous position,” he said.
The judge concluded with a stark warning for DOJ, however, after state officials complained that the Trump administration had made menacing comments about potentially prosecuting election workers who tabulated the votes of noncitizens: “This court believes it would be wise that any threats to state and county elected employees cease immediately.”
